AfriScan · Tanzania · Wayleaves, reserves and project areas

Know what is built inside your wayleave in Tanzania

We map structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground along pipelines, transmission lines, roads, railways and fibre routes, and inside mining and project areas. Each result is measured against your wayleave or reserve widths, dated, checked by a person and delivered as GIS files and a PDF report. Satellite first, with drone detail where a job needs it.

  • Your widthsThe wayleave, reserve or safety zone in your licence

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work Land Act, Cap. 113 · Electricity Act, Cap. 131 · Petroleum Act, Cap. 392 · Roads Act, 2007 · Railways Act, Cap. 170 · Civil Aviation (RPAS) Regulations, 2026 · Personal Data Protection Act, Cap. 44 · IFC Performance Standard 5

Why a dated record matters

Wayleaves bind everyone on the land

Tanzanian law protects pipeline, power-line, road and railway corridors in several statutes. They share one practical need: a dated, measured record of what stands inside the corridor.

Land Act, Cap. 113

A wayleave runs with the land

A wayleave created for the Government, a local authority, a public authority or a corporate body binds every occupier, under a right of occupancy, customary law or “as a trespasser”. The Commissioner for Lands can order an obstruction or encroachment on a public right of way removed, and failing to comply is an offence (ss.186–187).

Petroleum Act, Cap. 392

Pipelines and gas installations

A licensee acquires wayleaves around existing and future gas infrastructure and petroleum installations, and owners on or bordering a wayleave “shall not interfere” with the licensee’s rights (s.186).

Electricity Act, Cap. 131

Power lines

A licensee acquires a wayleave for its electricity facilities, owners on or bordering it must not interfere (s.37), and the licensee must remove or trim high vegetation that threatens safe operation (s.36(3)).

Roads Act · Railways Act

Roads and railways

The road reserve is “exclusive for the use of road development and expansion” (Roads Act, 2007, s.29), and the railway reserve runs 30 m either side of the track centre line (Railways Act, s.3).

Dates also decide compensation. The High Court has held that developments made after the valuation and notice are not compensable, and IFC Performance Standard 5 sets a cut-off date for lender-financed projects. When a structure first appeared can therefore matter as much as where it stands. Wayleave law in Tanzania, explained

What you receive

A dated register your wayleave, valuation and GIS teams can use

  • Structures, excavations and cleared ground, each with an ID, its distance to the centreline, its band, its chainage and its coordinates, counted by the widths you set and by route segment.
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low for encroachment density, so your wayleave officers know which stretches to visit first. It is a count rule, not a safety rating.
  • The imagery date and source for each feature, so the register can be read against a valuation or cut-off date.
  • Change since the last survey: new and removed structures, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.
  • A PDF report in English with maps, the segment table and the coordinate register, plus GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers and an interactive map file that opens in a browser.

Why it matters now

New corridors, and old ones in growing towns

Tanzania is building and planning long linear infrastructure while towns and villages grow towards the corridors it already has.

Oil

Crude and product pipelines

A cross-border crude pipeline, most of its length in Tanzania, is nearing completion and moving into operation, and new cross-border refined-products pipelines are being planned. A products pipeline built in the 1960s runs through towns that have grown up around it.

Power

A growing grid

Tanzania’s grid is growing, with new 400 kV and 220 kV lines and cross-border interconnectors. A 345 km 400 kV line was reported 99 per cent complete in August 2026, and a World Bank-financed programme covers about 620 km of 400 kV line in the south-west.

Rail

Railway land acquisition

A standard-gauge railway lot is acquiring land, with valuation, compensation and grave relocation along the route (utwaaji wa ardhi, uhamishaji wa makaburi).

Mining

Small-scale licence areas

The Mining Commission reported on 26 August 2026 that it had inspected 128 small-scale mining projects under technical-support agreements, found 42 inactive and 86 with shortcomings, and given 30 days to correct them.

Every one of these needs a record of what is on the ground: route options compared by the structures they affect, a baseline before valuation, and repeat surveys once the line is built.

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure is lawful is for you, the authorities and the courts to decide. Our registers support your wayleave, valuation, engagement and legal processes; they do not replace any of them.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one.

Neutral about communities

We write “structures in the wayleave”, “new construction”, “cleared ground” and “excavations”, and nothing about the people who live there.

Satellite first, drones where needed

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. Satellite mapping needs no drone permit and can start straight away, however long the corridor.

Drone detail. Where you need more detail than satellite imagery shows, we plan drone surveys under Tanzania’s 2026 drone regulations, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. Those regulations require an RPAS Operator Certificate from a company with a principal place of business registered in Tanzania, a security clearance and security programme, security-vetted pilots and TCAA’s authorisation for each operation, with a risk assessment submitted at least 14 days ahead.

Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals. Every drone proposal names the company that will fly and the approvals its flights rely on, so your team can check them.

The Tanzanian drone-law guide

GN 268 of 2026 regulation by regulation: the ROC, security vetting, the C2 frequency question, the 50 m rule along a wayleave, sensitive sites and an 11-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, as of 27 September 2026.

Drone law in Tanzania

For procurement and compliance teams

Local content, tenders and data

Oil and gas work in Tanzania carries the local-content rules of the Petroleum Act, s.219, mining work those of the Mining (Local Content) Regulations, and public buyers tender under the Public Procurement Act, 2023, through the national e-procurement system, NeST. Our notes set out what applies to this kind of service and what to ask any supplier for.

Working with AfriScan in Tanzania

We respond to RFQs and tenders. Send the tender or RFQ number and any prequalification forms with your request; each proposal states which company contracts, its local-content position for your contract, and how personal data are handled.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure?

Yours. Road and railway reserves are set in Tanzanian law, but the wayleave of a pipeline or power line comes from the licensee’s own acquisition, agreement or standard, and we found no single statutory width for either. Send the widths with the route, or the wayleave polygons themselves, and we report each structure’s distance to the line and the band it falls in, for example 0–15 m, 15–30 m and 30–60 m, with up to six widths in one survey.

How recent is the imagery?

As recent as the dated imagery for your area allows. We start from dated very-high-resolution archive scenes or the imagery you hold, and request a new satellite capture where the archive is too old. Every report names its imagery and, where the source gives it, the capture date. New captures depend on satellite availability and weather, so no capture date is ever guaranteed.

Do you need drones?

Not usually. Satellite mapping needs no drone permit, no launch sites and no one on site, and it covers a whole corridor. Drone surveys add detail where a stretch needs it, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. See drone law in Tanzania.

Can you tell whether a structure is lawful?

No. We map what stands where, and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether it is inside a wayleave lawfully, predates the wayleave or valuation, or is compensable is for your land team, the valuers, the Commissioner for Lands and the courts to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

How is personal data handled?

Our registers describe structures and ground, not people, and carry no names. Lists of project-affected persons and drone frames that show people are personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act, so each contract says who processes them, where they are stored and how any transfer outside Tanzania is covered (ss.31–32).

Is the register a cadastral survey?

No. It is a mapping and monitoring record built from imagery. Title boundaries, beacons and survey plans stay with land surveyors; the register shows them, your wayleave officers and your valuers where to look.

Know what stands in your wayleave while it is still one structure.

Send the route or site file (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the regions it crosses and the wayleave, reserve or safety-zone widths from your own licence or agreement. If a valuation or cut-off date applies, tell us. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
